summary: HERO is an RL recipe for coding agents with two parts: a resolution-first objective that only turns on a token-efficiency reward once the policy solves enough tasks, and credit assignment at two levels (shorter successful trajectories, and penalties on low-entropy 'unproductive' turns). Qwen3.5-4B/9B/35B-A3B are trained on 640 multilingual SWE tasks inside the Claude Code scaffold and evaluated on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Average resolve rate rises from 37.4% to 42.2%, using 39.8% fewer tokens than GRPO.

claims.claim: HERO raises average resolve rate from 37.4% to 42.2% across the Qwen3.5 variants.
claims.evidence: Averaging the six base cells in Tables 1-2 gives 37.4 and the six HERO cells gives 42.2, so the claim matches. Results are the mean of 3 seeds (§4.1), but no std or CI is given. Per-cell gains are 1.4-7.2 points.

claims.claim: HERO matches or beats GRPO on resolve rate with 39.8% less token usage.
claims.evidence: GRPO tokens sum to 36.9M across the six cells and HERO to 22.2M (about 40% less), so the arithmetic holds. Against the untrained base model, however, HERO uses 22.2M vs 23.4M, only about 5% fewer, and more on Multilingual-4B (4.5 vs 4.0). The 'efficiency' is largely undoing GRPO's token inflation, not reducing below baseline.

claims.claim: HERO beats token-efficient RL baselines (Training Efficient, LASER, OTC-GRPO, SlimSearcher).
claims.evidence: Table 6 on Qwen3.5-4B only. HERO has the best TRS, but LASER and OTC-GRPO use fewer tokens with lower resolve. Baselines were re-implemented by the authors with configs copied from papers designed for non-SWE settings (LASER threshold chosen by the authors).

claims.claim: Each component matters: removing hierarchical policy optimization collapses resolve to 29.2%.

claims.evidence: Table 12: under mini-SWE-agent, 4B goes 39.5 (base), 41.2 (GRPO), 43.0 (HERO). Only one alternative scaffold and one model size. Notably, the base model scores higher in mini-SWE-agent than in Claude Code (39.5 vs 32.8).

patterns.note: RL with an efficiency reward gated on capability improves resolve over the base model and keeps tokens near base, avoiding the token inflation seen with plain GRPO.
Shows token cost can be trained down, but HERO's tokens are close to the base model's. Inference-time caps (turn limit, masking) reduce tokens but not resolve rate (App. B.2).
Inference-time pruning and masking are compared (App. B.2) and found complementary to, not substitutes for, training.

methodology.sample: Training: 640 tasks from SWE-Gym, Multi-SWE-bench and SWE-rebench (352 Python, 38 Java, 50 each in C/C++, JS/TS, PHP, Go, Rust). Evaluation: SWE-bench Verified 500 and Multilingual 300.
methodology.baselines: GRPO (no efficiency term), four token-efficient RL methods re-implemented by the authors, four inference-time methods, and four open-source coding models (Gemma-4-26B-A4B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash, KAT-Dev-32B) run in the Claude Code scaffold.
methodology.models: Qwen3.5-4B, 9B, 35B-A3B (one model family). Most ablations use 4B only.
methodology.variance: 3 seeds, means only; no std, CIs or significance.
methodology.ablations: Component ablations, lambda sweep, capability threshold and entropy percentile sensitivity, scaffold transfer (4B).
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed. Training draws from Multi-SWE-bench and SWE-rebench; possible repository overlap with SWE-bench Multilingual is not addressed.
methodology.languages: Multilingual training and evaluation (nine languages in SWE-bench Multilingual). No per-language breakdown, and Java has only 38 training tasks.

standards.artifacts: No code, checkpoints or training data link found.

biases.detail: The headline 39.8% token saving is measured against GRPO, which has no efficiency term and inflates tokens. Against the base model the saving is about 5%.
3 seeds but only means; margins of 1-3 points on 300-500 tasks are reported without dispersion.
Only the Qwen3.5 family is trained; ablations are on 4B only.
No discussion of overlap between SWE-bench (Verified/Multilingual) and the training sources, or of pretraining exposure.
The TRS trade-off metric and the 'unproductive behavior' identification (App. A.4) are the authors' own constructs, used to score their own method.

coi.affiliations: Haobin Li, Zhenyu Huang, Mouxing Yang and Xi Peng (Sichuan University); Liang Jiang (independent researcher). The regex 'GitHub' hit is a false positive from benchmark text.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Claude Code is used as the scaffold only; Qwen is the backbone and is not the authors' product.

verdict_reason: The abstract numbers match the tables, there are seeds and broad baselines, and evaluation is multilingual. But the token saving is framed against an inflating GRPO baseline (about 5% vs base), only one model family is used, no dispersion is reported, contamination is unaddressed, and no artifacts are released.
applicability: Low direct use. The team will not RL-train its own coding model, and mixed hosts use vendor models. The transferable observations are about harness telemetry. Repeated tool calls, over-exploration and erroneous commands are measurable 'unproductive turn' signals the harness can log and flag. Inference-time turn caps or masking cut tokens without raising resolve rate (App. B.2), so a budget cap alone won't improve quality. It also flags that RL-tuned open models can be much more token-hungry (GRPO rows), which matters if the team routes cheap tasks to open-weight models. Java coverage is thin (38 training tasks, no per-language results).
